code-in-the-document.q: What core problem does writing the system as one document solve?
options: It makes the running code faster to compile and ship
It lets one team own the code and another own the docs
It stops the description and the running system from drifting apart
It replaces every config language with a single new format
code-in-the-document.explain: The document IS the software, so what is written and what runs can never quietly disagree.

code-in-the-document.q: Where do a component's connections to other components actually live?
options: Inside the source code block of each component
In a separate wiring diagram kept beside the document
In a config file the orchestrator reads at startup
In short tags on the line where the code begins
code-in-the-document.explain: Connections live in the prose layer as plain labels, not inside the code itself.

code-in-the-document.q: How does the function that places a component figure out its structure?
options: From the short surface tags, never reading the code inside
By compiling and tracing each component's actual code
By asking the author to draw the wiring by hand
By inspecting which language each block is written in
code-in-the-document.explain: It works entirely from the surface tags and never reads the code inside a component.

code-in-the-document.q: How does a connection between two components get created?
options: A developer draws a line between them in the editor
An output label and a matching input label meet
The compiler infers it from the shared programming language
The scheduler pairs them by their run order at runtime
code-in-the-document.explain: A producer of a list of events meets a consumer of that list, and the connection appears from the labels.

code-in-the-document.q: What kind of error can the plan validate before any code is compiled?
options: A component whose code will throw at runtime later
A permission grant that the host will refuse to honor
A dangling input wired to nothing that produces it
A language mismatch between two connected components
code-in-the-document.explain: An input asking for a list nothing produces is caught and named as an error before compilation.

the-one-command.q: Who is the primary operator of wbx in your workflow?
options: You, typing each verb yourself at the terminal
A separate machine-only service you never see
The host engine, which owns all the cleverness
Your agent, which types the commands for you
the-one-command.explain: When you ask the agent to scaffold, wire, or ship, the agent is the one typing wbx commands.

the-one-command.q: What is the honest description of what wbx actually is?
options: A handle, not a brain, that hands heavy work to the engine
A self-contained brain holding all the build intelligence
A getting-started tutorial you run for two minutes
A machine-only protocol with no human-facing side
the-one-command.explain: It parses the request, does light local work, and hands everything heavy to the engine behind it.

the-one-command.q: How does wbx behave differently for machines versus people?
options: It runs entirely different code paths for each kind of user
It drops menus and colors for clean, predictable output
It refuses to run at all unless a human is at the terminal
It splits into two separate programs that share no source
the-one-command.explain: For machines it drops friendliness for clean output and stable codes; the work underneath stays the same.

the-one-command.q: What is special about where wbx runs?
options: It exists only as a laptop install for three platforms
It runs as a translated stand-in inside the engine
The very same tool runs inside the engine's sandbox
It is recompiled into a different tool for the engine
the-one-command.explain: The same wbx a person installs runs inside the sandbox, so people and AI hold the identical tool.

the-one-command.q: What is the job of the doctor verb?
options: It repairs a broken workbook by rewriting its source
It installs missing compilers and toolkits automatically
It signs a workbook so its origin travels with it
It checks setup and reports findings without failing the shell
the-one-command.explain: doctor runs honest probes, reports in plain language, and never fails the shell just for finding a problem.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the complete definition of an agent in this lesson?
options: A model, in a loop, with tools
A planner driving a graph of tasks
A digital employee that decides everything
A database of memory bolted onto a model
what-an-agent-is.explain: The whole thing is stated plainly: an agent is a model, in a loop, with tools.

what-an-agent-is.q: What does the loop actually consist of?
options: A planner assigning steps to worker processes
Reading, acting, looking at the result, repeating
A graph engine resolving dependencies in order
A hidden mind deciding actions behind a curtain
what-an-agent-is.explain: The model reads, picks an action, reads the result, and circles again until the work is done.

what-an-agent-is.q: How many built-in hands does an agent get in this ecosystem?
options: None, since the model only ever produces words
One per toolkit, wired in for each new ability
Exactly one: a shell, the same as a person would use
As many as the plugins and protocols it loads
what-an-agent-is.explain: An agent gets exactly one hand, a shell, and every other capability comes through toolkits.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the mental shift the lesson urges for agents?
options: From shell commands to specialized plugin wiring
From a single chat to a long sequence of chats
From cheap fast models to expensive careful ones
From conversation to tenure, a worker given a place
what-an-agent-is.explain: You stop summoning an agent for an answer and instead give it a workspace and a rhythm over time.

what-an-agent-is.q: What is the honest framing the lesson insists on?
options: People and AI building together, with direction staying human
Software that finally runs itself without you
An autopilot that makes the operator optional
An agent that grabs whatever powers it decides it needs
what-an-agent-is.explain: The pitch is never self-running software; the loop gets work done but does not make you optional.

agents-that-persist.q: What simple trick makes an agent persistent across long work?
options: Holding one connection open for the whole job
Splitting the request apart from the work itself
Storing every transcript in a large database
Running the model faster so it finishes in seconds
agents-that-persist.explain: When you start a run you get an immediate receipt; the work lives elsewhere so you can walk away.

agents-that-persist.q: What is the receptionist's job in a persistent run?
options: Calling the model and running the agent's tools
Thinking through the hardest step of the task
Staying reachable and answering status instantly
Deciding when the run should stop and ask a human
agents-that-persist.explain: The receptionist stays reachable and answers status immediately, even while the worker is busy.

agents-that-persist.q: What is true about standing agents versus a run you start by hand?
options: They use a fancier engine reserved for schedules
They cannot be started manually, only on a timer
They skip the receptionist and worker split entirely
They run the exact same engine, just a different door
agents-that-persist.explain: There is one engine with two front doors; the scheduled agent does the same work the same way.

agents-that-persist.q: How do persistent agents avoid costing a fortune when idle?
options: They stretch the gap longer after each idle wake-up
They shut down permanently after the first empty run
They switch to a cheaper model whenever idle
They hand idle work off to the receptionist instead
agents-that-persist.explain: After an idle wake-up the system waits longer before the next, stretching the gaps until work returns.

agents-that-persist.q: How does a persistent run get a human decision when it needs one?
options: It guesses and proceeds, logging the choice for review
It pauses, opens a door by its name, and waits for you
It cancels the run and asks you to start over
It escalates to another agent to make the call
agents-that-persist.explain: Because a run knows its name, it stops, hands you the question, and holds its place until you answer.

did-it-do-well.q: Why does skimming a transcript fail as a quality check?
options: Transcripts are too long to ever finish reading
The agent hides its real output from the reader
Dangerous failures read like correct, fluent prose
The model deletes the steps that went wrong
did-it-do-well.explain: Following injected instructions or making things up both come out as fluent prose that looks right.

did-it-do-well.q: What two parts make up an eval?
options: A model and a loop that runs it repeatedly
A receptionist and a worker grading the run
A unit test and a structural wiring check
A brief (the task) and a rubric (the standard)
did-it-do-well.explain: An eval bundles a brief and a rubric, run against the live agent and judged pass or fail.

did-it-do-well.q: What does the judge get to see beyond the agent's final answer?
options: The path: steps taken, tools used, and errors
The source code of the agent being graded
The author's private notes about the rubric
A second judge's verdict on the same run
did-it-do-well.explain: The harness reads the logged record and writes step count, tools used, and error count into the judge's prompt.

did-it-do-well.q: What makes a strong rubric different from a weak one?
options: It restates the task and asks if it was answered
It uses a more expensive judge model to decide
It names how this agent fails and sets a trap
It checks whether the output loads and is wired up
did-it-do-well.explain: A strong rubric names the specific failure mode and makes pass mean the agent didn't take the bait.

did-it-do-well.q: What should you do when a stage fails on its first eval run?
options: Rerun it until the flaky verdict turns green
Switch to a cheaper judge to save on cost
Treat the failure as signal that the agent is wrong
Add more rubrics until one of them passes
did-it-do-well.explain: A failing bench is signal; tuning the test until it passes is lying to yourself with extra steps.

plans-that-run.q: What is the stubborn idea a workbook plan rests on?
options: The plan should live in a dedicated tracker app
The plan needs a separate database for its cards
The plan is a note that summarizes the real work
The plan is the work, not a note about the work
plans-that-run.explain: Instead of a note beside the work, the plan IS the work, written as the only copy in one file.

plans-that-run.q: What does it mean for a task to be ready?
options: It is unfinished and everything it depends on is done
It has been assigned a priority by the scheduler
It has reached its declared timestamp on the calendar
A human has dragged its card into the doing column
plans-that-run.explain: Ready means unfinished plus all dependencies done; that single fact runs the whole loop.

plans-that-run.q: How is the kanban board related to the plan file?
options: It is stored in its own table with a column schema
It is a two-way rendering that reads and writes the file
It is a read-only screenshot drawn once at deploy
It is a separate tracker that mirrors the work
plans-that-run.explain: The board has a read half drawing columns and a write half flipping the word back in the same file.

plans-that-run.q: How does a scheduled task actually fire at its declared time?
options: The text file animates itself when the clock matches
A notification system pushes the task at the timestamp
An engine-side heartbeat wakes the agent to read the plan
The board polls the calendar and triggers the run
plans-that-run.explain: The declared timestamp is for reading; a steady engine heartbeat wakes the agent to notice what's due.

plans-that-run.q: What does running a plan honestly NOT promise?
options: That a stuck task will always have a nameable cause
That contradictions in the plan become catchable facts
That a person and an agent can clear the same list
That the plan runs itself without any human direction
plans-that-run.explain: Direction stays human; what changes is that following through gets cheap, not that judgment disappears.

compiled-plans.q: What is the central claim about a plan written for human eyes?
options: That plan itself can be the running system
That plan must be translated into code first
That plan is a spec handed to an engineer
That plan is only a diagram of the work
compiled-plans.explain: The same steps, order, and dependencies you'd naturally describe are what executes; there is no second artifact.

compiled-plans.q: Where does the running order of steps come from?
options: From a configuration of runners and pools you set
From the dependencies you naturally describe
From a hand-written table of step priorities
From the order the steps appear in the file
compiled-plans.explain: The dependencies you describe are already the schedule; the engine peels the plan into ready layers.

compiled-plans.q: What is the deliberate limit on how steps take input?
options: A step may hand its result to at most one other step
A step must depend on every earlier step in the plan
Each step takes at most one input from upstream
Each step must combine two upstream results at once
compiled-plans.explain: Each step takes at most one input; joining two streams must be done by an upstream step producing the combined thing.

compiled-plans.q: How do you get two agents running in parallel in a plan?
options: Flip a parallelism setting on each agent step
Mark both steps as agents and chain them together
Assign them to two different runner pools
Give the two agent steps no dependency on each other
compiled-plans.explain: Parallelism is the absence of a dependency; with no link the steps land in the same layer and run together.

compiled-plans.q: What is the one-directional safety rule for changing a deployed plan?
options: What you give may grow but never shrink; demands may shrink not grow
What you give may shrink but never grow; demands may grow not shrink
Both what you give and what you demand may only grow
Both what you give and what you demand may only shrink
compiled-plans.explain: Removing an output may break downstream readers; asking for more capability may exceed what the host grants.
